editorial.headline: Post-Harvest Services With a Clear Bali Path
editorial.standfirst: A contract-based activity for preparing agricultural outputs for primary markets, open across all business scales and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
KBLI 01630 covers the practical work that happens after cultivation but before agricultural goods enter the primary market. Its centre of gravity is service: post-harvest activity carried out for a fee or under contract, rather than the farmer’s own preparation of the crop. In plain English, this is the business of making agricultural outputs sale-ready without turning them into a different industrial product. The record names cleaning, sorting, grading, peeling, sun drying, and disinfection as core examples, alongside more specific work such as separating cotton seed, preparing tobacco leaves by sun drying, peeling cocoa beans, waxing fruit, and naturally drying fruit, vegetables, spices, and medicinal herbs.

The scope is broader than a single commodity line. It can include sorting, cleaning, and cutting medicinal herbs; retting textile fibre plants such as jute, flax, or coir where that work is not part of the cultivation activity itself; and artificial ripening of fruit as a service, with banana ripening given as the example. That range matters because the classification is not defined by one product, but by the role the operator performs in the agricultural chain: a post-harvest contractor preparing goods for sale at the primary-market stage. The boundary is also clear from the record. It is not ordinary preparation done by the farmer, not seed-quality improvement, not commission or cooperative marketing, not wholesale trade, not oil production from grains, and not research into new seed forms.

For registration scale, the record is unusually straightforward. The activity is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That means the classification can describe anything from a small contracted sorting operation to a larger service facility handling multiple agricultural outputs, as long as the work remains within the post-harvest service scope set out above. Nationally, the foreign-investment status is also clear: it is marked TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%, sourced to Perpres 10/2021 and 49/2021. There is no partial cap in the slim record, so the national reading is not a restricted-foreign-stake reading; it is a fully open PMA reading at the level stated in the record.

The Bali picture is equally important, because many otherwise open activities fail at the provincial gate. Here, however, the record does not show a Bali block. The Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the stated reason is that OSS risk at Besar scale is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, so it is not blocked by the Bali moratorium. The moratorium rule in the record is severe: Bali province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA island-wide, permanently. But this activity, on the record supplied, does not fall into the blocked side of that rule. The honest conclusion is therefore clean: nationally it is open to 100% foreign ownership, and in Bali it is not blocked by the stated PMA moratorium.
